content: Prevpac is a combination therapy consisting of lansoprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin. It is used for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori to reduce the risk of duodenal ulcer recurrence. The recommended dosage includes lansoprazole 30 mg, amoxicillin 1 g, and clarithromycin 500 mg, administered orally twice daily (morning and evening) for a duration of 10 or 14 days. Each dose contains four pills: one capsule of lansoprazole (30 mg), two capsules of amoxicillin (500 mg each), and one tablet of clarithromycin (500 mg). The packaging is clearly labeled to facilitate proper administration of one dose (30 mg/1 g/500 mg) twice daily. In patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min), Prevpac should not be used. For patients with hepatic impairment, no dosage adjustment is required. However, the safety and efficacy of this therapy have not been fully established in all populations. During treatment, there is a potential risk of superinfections caused by fungal or bacterial pathogens. If superinfections occur, the therapy should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Prescribing this therapy in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and may increase the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Serious adverse reactions have been reported with clarithromycin when used concurrently with CYP3A4 substrates. These include colchicine toxicity when used with colchicine, rhabdomyolysis when used with simvastatin, lovastatin, or atorvastatin, hypoglycemia when used with disopyramide, and hypotension or acute kidney injury when used with calcium channel blockers metabolized by CYP3A4 (e.g., verapamil, amlodipine, diltiazem, nifedipine). Most cases of acute kidney injury associated with calcium channel blockers occurred in elderly patients aged 65 years or older. Clarithromycin should be used cautiously when co-administered with medications that induce the CYP3A4 enzyme. Caution is also advised when clarithromycin is administered to nursing women. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for clarithromycin and the potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Clarithromycin is generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category A), as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. The drug is highly stable in the presence of gastric acid, unlike erythromycin. Food may delay its absorption but does not affect the extent of absorption. Clarithromycin is widely distributed into most body tissues except the central nervous system. It is partially metabolized in the liver (via the CYP3A4 enzyme) and converted to an active metabolite, 14-OH clarithromycin. The drug is primarily excreted in the urine, with renal clearance approximating normal glomerular filtration rates. Its half-life ranges from 3 to 7 hours, depending on the formulation (immediate-release or extended-release). The enteric-coated granules in the formulation are acid-labile and should not be chewed or crushed. For optimal therapeutic outcomes, adherence to the prescribed regimen is essential.
